o: We need two independent answers combined into one result column: (1) the user who rated the most movies, breaking ties by lexicographically smallest name, and (2) the movie with the highest average rating during February 2020, again ties broken by lexicographically smaller title. In the example, Daniel and Monica both rated 3 movies, so Daniel wins alphabetically; Frozen 2 and Joker both average 3.5 in February 2020, so Frozen 2 wins. Since this is a pure aggregation problem over three tables, the natural tool is GROUP BY with COUNT/AVG plus ORDER BY for tie-breaking, then LIMIT 1 per sub-question, UNIONed together.
k: Each of the two questions is an independent aggregate: group by user_id (or movie_id), compute count (or average), sort by metric DESC then name ASC, take one row.
UNION ALL combines two single-row results into the required 'results' column.
February 2020 filtering can be done with DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m') = '2020-02' or a range predicate created_at >= '2020-02-01' AND created_at < '2020-03-01'.

a.n: Approach 1: Two grouped subqueries with ORDER BY + LIMIT, UNIONed
a.i: Group MovieRating by user_id joined to Users to get each user's rating count; order by count descending, name ascending, and keep the first row. Do the analogous thing for movies restricted to February 2020 using AVG(rating). UNION ALL the two one-row results since both share a single varchar output column.
s: Join Users with MovieRating, GROUP BY user_id, compute COUNT(*) as cnt.
ORDER BY cnt DESC, name ASC and LIMIT 1 to get the top rater with lexicographic tie-break.
Filter ratings to February 2020, join Movies, GROUP BY movie_id, compute AVG(rating).
ORDER BY average DESC, title ASC, LIMIT 1 for the best February movie.
Combine both results with UNION ALL.

c.python:
(SELECT u.name AS results
FROM Users u
JOIN MovieRating m ON u.user_id = m.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, u.name ASC
LIMIT 1)
UNION ALL
(SELECT mo.title AS results
FROM Movies mo
JOIN MovieRating mr ON mo.movie_id = mr.movie_id
WHERE mr.created_at >= '2020-02-01' AND mr.created_at < '2020-03-01'
GROUP BY mo.movie_id, mo.title
ORDER BY AVG(mr.rating) DESC, mo.title ASC
LIMIT 1);

a.t: O(R log R) where R is the number of rows in MovieRating — grouping is linear and sorting for tie-breaking dominates.
a.sp: O(U + M) extra space for the grouped intermediate results, where U and M are the numbers of users and movies.

a.n: Approach 2: Window functions (RANK) instead of ORDER BY/LIMIT
a.i: Compute aggregates in CTEs, then assign RANK() ordered by metric DESC and name ASC; select rank = 1 from each CTE and UNION ALL. This generalizes cleanly if you ever need all tied winners or top-k per group.
s: CTE user_counts: join Users and MovieRating, group by user, count ratings.
Rank users by count DESC, name ASC using RANK().
CTE feb_avg: filter to Feb 2020, join Movies, group by movie, average rating.
Rank movies by avg DESC, title ASC.
Select rank-1 rows from both CTEs and UNION ALL them.

c.python:
WITH uc AS (
  SELECT u.name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, u.name ASC) AS rk
  FROM Users u JOIN MovieRating m ON u.user_id = m.user_id
  GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name
),
ma AS (
  SELECT mo.title, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(mr.rating) DESC, mo.title ASC) AS rk
  FROM Movies mo JOIN MovieRating mr ON mo.movie_id = mr.movie_id
  WHERE mr.created_at >= '2020-02-01' AND mr.created_at < '2020-03-01'
  GROUP BY mo.movie_id, mo.title
)
SELECT name AS results FROM uc WHERE rk = 1
UNION ALL
SELECT title FROM ma WHERE rk = 1;

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it is short, idiomatic SQL, and directly expresses 'top one with tie-break' via ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1. Use the window-function version when asked to generalize to returning all tied winners or top-k groups. Common pitfalls: forgetting the lexicographic tie-break (must appear as the second ORDER BY key), filtering dates incorrectly (use a half-open range rather than MONTH()/YEAR() on the raw column so indexes can still help), and using UNION instead of UNION ALL (harmless here but semantically wrong intent). Edge cases: no ratings at all (queries return empty — acceptable per constraints), and ties in counts or averages which the name ordering resolves. Follow-ups might ask for top-k raters/movies or monthly best movies, which the window-function approach handles naturally with PARTITION BY month.
